## 4. Psycho Goreman (2020)

**Score:** 54
**Body:** Saw that this movie is free on Tubi and decided to watch it last night. It's hilarious, violent, and just absolutely insane.

The movie is about a fearsome intergalactic warrior who falls under control of a ten year old girl. The comedy mixes sci-fi action with body horror. The special effects make it look like if someone crossed Power Rangers with the band GWAR.

A special shout-out to Nita-Josee Hanna as the girl Mimi. Her character is just bizarre in the best way possible that makes her the Nicholas Cage of child actors. I don't know if she's intentionally bad, but she's certainly amusing manipulating a homicidal alien and being a weird child.

If you're looking for a movie that's pure unadulterated fun, this is it. Perfect for just watching with some friends while inebriated and eating pizza on a late night to give it an insane slumber party vibe

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. The greatest movie sequel of all time.

**Score:** 305
**Body:** Yes its a subjective opinion but I'd also like to defend it a little.

The Godfather Part 2 and the LOTR Two Towers are both works of art, yes. But the fact is these were adaptations of popular books, with the same director and creative team as the first. They were basically slam dunks. Follow the storytelling style of the first, you cant go wrong.

Aliens was the brainchild of James Cameron. He was following up arguably the best sci fi horror film of all time, with nothing written for him. For most directors thats a hospital pass. (It certainly was for David Fincher and Alien 3). He couldnt copy the original, that would have made it a lazy cashgrab. But he also had to keep it in that world, it needed to be recognizably Alien.

The fact Cameron managed to surpass the original in a lot of ways, putting his own stamp on it, is a moviemaking miracle. Particuarly with the behind the scenes difficulties, squabbles with the crew at Pinewood, and Fox not believing in the film at all at first. And that it was made on a relatively modest budget of $18 million.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. ![gif](giphy|9S3L4JDX7cKuk)
  - ![gif](giphy|U6U4LSZTQiCKOtnooa)
  - I like how James Cameron is basically doing battle with himself in this scenario.

And yeah I agree with both tbh
  - This is the most appropriate use of a gif that i have ever seen. Two birds with one stone, excellent choice.
  - It is really hard to argue against T2.  This movie is so good that it far exceeds the original, which in itself is awesome.  
2. The Empire Strikes Back would like a word
  - The Empire Strikes Back is EXACTLY a perfect sequel. It continues the story of the first one WITHOUT repeating it.

That is what I always hope for in a sequel. I want to see what happens next to the characters. I don't want to see the same thing happen to the characters again.
3. The Dark Knight
4. The Wrath of Khan was so good the folks behind the Star Trek films have been trying to replicate it ever since. 
5. >*The fact Cameron managed to surpass the original in a lot of ways...*

The original has not been surpassed in any way.

## 2. Finally watched Primetime, Pattinson is phenomenal

**Score:** 241

But what he does in Primetime is transformative. Everything from the cadence to the gestures is so convincing, I was blown away. He knows how to do intensity and how to do restrain.

The storytelling and stylistic choices were divisive amongst my buddies and I, but we all agreed that Pattinson was aces in the role. 

A24 and Pattinson are a match made in heaven. One of the best performances in Robert’s career!

https://preview.redd.it/pnhhdd8ehwrh1.jpeg?width=600&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=46dc2d703717d5d334408d9cbc043ddbab253a39
3. Absolutely, the T-Rex showdown goes hard. 

The planes sequence gets me in the feels. 
4. I think all of Kong stuff still looks great. I think the scene when they’re running from the dinosaurs looks horrible but I thought it looked confusingly bad when it came out too
5. Just like other Weta projects in that era there’s stuff that aged fine and other things that look meh today. 
6. Yes. That whole lineup at the Oscars for visual effects, War Of The Worlds and Narnia holds up. 2005-2007 vfx were peak 
7. Its a real mix bag of a film in that regard.

 Kong looks phenomenal even now. Skull Island itself, the village, the ship and 1930s New York are super convincing. The trex fight, spider pit and log scene are still impressive, as is the swamp scene in the extended cut. 

But then there's the infamous brontosaurus stampede, which looks shockingly bad (even at the time it looked a bit naff). And the sacrifice scene has bad fire effects and native sprites on the wall, and there's bad crewman sprites when they capture Kong. The bat scene looks really bad too.

Basically its a film that mostly holds up, but you can tell they only had 2 years to make it.

## 5. What movie do you consider really good, but perfectly understand why someone might not like it?

**Score:** 143
**Body:** For me it would be “*The Wolf of Wall Street”*

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Place Beyond the Pines 
  - the way they switch between dads feels kinda jarring but fits the story
2. Substance (2024). The amount of ass shots in that movie is too much.
3. Midsommar 
  - What I really liked is the first part, before the title, as that is just the most horrifying thing I can imagine ever happening to me and Florence Pugh played it so well it nearly causes a panic attack to me every time
4. Actually anything Tarantino. But for me it’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.

This is a movie with a plot of nothing and a message of everything. It’s a love letter to an era I’m also deeply in love with. I feel every scene a masterpiece, but I can easily see how many would look at it as a boring mess that’s way too long.

Really a hit or miss, as if you’re enjoying less action, slow and steady character building you’ll like it, if you’re more into contemporary, action filled Hollywood you may find it boring.
5. This is the first I was aware that people didn’t like this movie. 
  - I've definitely seen people say they don't like it because it glorifies the culture of greed, selfishness and debauchery of wall street in the 80s and 90s. 

That obviously wasn't Scorsese's intention, he was trying to show how empty and soulless that culture was, but there's definitely a certain type of guy who completely missed the point and saw Belfort as a hero and role model. 
6. Some people don't like English humour, and many dislike zombie movies, but this is a top five comedy for me.

![gif](giphy|MXoz4MqhUYinsJ5bEz)
7. Fargo. I watched it with five other people and I’m the only one who liked it.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. My second watch of Mulholland Drive

**Score:** 1
**Body:** First of all sorry for my english since it is not my first lenguaje. And please dont give me the clearcut answers (if they exist) to this movie. I am posting this manly because David Lynch himself said it was a good idea to talk about his movies with other people to understand them and i have no friends (jk). 

I saw for the first time Mulholland Drive this week. I usually dont rewatch movies so close to my first viewing but after thinking about it I had some new theories and i wanted to confirm it or see if i was close to a better understanding. After watching it again i am sure that i am very far to really understand the movie but i enjoyed it much more on my second watch knowing what the movie was about and having some clues to understand it.

At a superficial look at the movie is clear that it is very interesed in acting and identity. I think there is a very interesting dichotomy between Betty and Rita. After Betty gave her the wig and they were going to sleep she told her that she didnt had to put their wig when there was only the two of them. I think this is a reference that to Betty having a clear identity she is able (and loves) to put on other identities but only to show the people around it. To her it is basically a game. But to Rita this game of acting is an act inwards. Since she doesnt had a clear identity to her putting a wig is to signal to herself what she is. In this case she was trying to put the identity of Diane.

I think another interesting detail is when Betty is practicing her rol she act very differently depending of who was acting with her. The old guy said to her "Acting is reacting". I think this line is not only true in acting but it is meant to be about our identities. We always change our behaviour or personality (even how we understand ourselfs) depending on the interlocutor since our identities only make sense in relantionship to other people. 

And obviously the movie is really meta. The "silence club" i am very sure it was called that because when you go to the cinema they ask you to be silent. And the guy there was talking about how the movie you are watching is fake.

My original theory was that the second half after they open the box the movie became a movie inside a movie (the movie that Adam was making). The cowboy said that if Adam doesnt chose the girl ("Camila Rhodes") the cowboy would appear two more times and in the movie after the first appearence he appears two more times. Also based on the look he gave to Betty i think it is safe to asume Adam chose Betty as the leading role instead of "Camila Rhodes".

I think i am right about this but there is still a lot of open questions. Of course i know being a David Lynch movie probably a lot of this questions doesnt have a clear cut answer but still it is interesting to ponder. Now of course there are a lot of evidence that Camila Rhodes and Rita are actually the same person (i dont think the same for Diane and Betty). We saw how Diane was planning her murder (that didnt work) at the end of movie and also how Camila take the keys he had in her bag at the start of the movie. Also of course the "real Camila Rhodes" doesnt look latina at all. I originally thought she was someone in the original relationship between Diane and Camilla. Maybe Diane trying to steal his identity after the relationship ended. But we are sure Diane is dead and Camilla is Rita so who really is she?

This is my most crackpot theory yet but maybe the movie is more meta that it seems at first and the way "Camilla" take the identity of Camilla instead of just inside the movie inside a movie but also in the reality outside the movie. Basically she stole the real identity and change reality making this movie impossible to understand.

This are my thoughts so far. Sorry if it my rambling werent coherent but even if i didnt understand fully (or at all) i really like this movie and i really enjoy watching a movie that challenges you to be understood.

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I would also have to watch a second time before I could even speculate. I just recently watched Lost Highway, Mulholland, and Inland Empire all in a row and it's interesting how similar some of the story beats are. Not a downside, just interesting. 
  - The well-discussed meme about Lost Highway is that no one understood it originally, so Lynch felt free to re-use the same story concept in Mulholland Drive.

## 2. Kim Ki-duk rivals Martin Scorsese’s Taxi Driver with Moebius

**Score:** 1
**Body:** Just watched **Moebius**, I honestly think it can be compared to **Taxi Driver** in terms of how bleak, disturbing and psychologically extreme it gets.

* Extremely grim atmosphere
* Next-level violence and brutality
* Women are portrayed through prostitution and sexual exploitation
* A deeply uncomfortable exploration of sex, shame and repression
* But **Moebius** has a more philosophical vibe, whereas **Taxi Driver** feels more grounded in urban alienation and psychological deterioration

Both films feel like they’re taking you into the darkest parts of human behavior, but they approach it from very different angles. **Moebius** is almost like a nightmare or philosophical parable rather than a conventional psychological drama.

Curious if anyone else sees the connection between Kim Ki-duk and Scorsese here.

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. There is no comparison to be made. Moebius comes across as some sort of perverted sexual male fantasy played out on film. Knowing the Director's sexual assault charges directly related to *this* film as well as other projects adds weight to the exploitative nature and tone of Moebius.

I've liked other films by him but comparing this film to Taxi Driver is a severe misinterpretation of both films.
2. Kim Ki Duk is my favorite Korean film maker, and one of my favorite directors generally. His movie '*3-Iron*' is my favorite from his catalogue, and I think it's the best directed movie I've personally seen.   
  
I also really enjoyed '*Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring*' and '*The Net*'. 
3. If anything, late Kim Ki-duk rivals early Kim Ki-duk. Both *Pieta* and *Arirang* are kind of up there with *Crocodile* and maybe *The Bow*, but that's it.

Other than that, Kim Ki-duk's work is nowhere near a masterpiece like *Taxi Driver*.

'**Moebius** has a more philosophical vibe' is just too misleading a sentence. I fail to think in something more philosophical than the midnight convo between the Wizard and Travis.

## 3. Could Kubrick's portrayal of HAL 9000 be interpreted as a critique of technological advancement and AI?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** First, I have to say (and this will probably lead to a lot of downvotes) that I didn't particularly enjoy 2001: A Space Odyssey. I'm an (almost) literature graduate, and I care a lot about the story and characters in a movie, and I like to analyze movies like books and stories and focus on the plot, themes, messages, and ideas. And while 2001 was visually incredible and was probably mind-blowing back when it was released, I couldn't really get the story and analyze it as well as I could. I'm a huge fan of Kubrick's work (Paths of Glory, FMJ, and The Shining are among my favorite movies ever). But I couldn't really get the visual storytelling and the abstruse nature of the plot in 2001. This is probably mostly a problem on my end, as my mind just seems to work a lot more efficiently with words and sentences than visuals.

But the ''Jupiter Mission'' section of the movie, particularly the behavior of HAL, really seemed like a cautionary tale to me. The fact that HAL tried to "sacrifice" every human on the spaceship because it thought that it was a completely faultless device and that its disconnection would lead to the end of a very important mission I think represents the danger of creating an emotionless entity without empathy (''the danger'' being the demise of humanity). I think Kubrick shows that our perceived imperfections (emotions and empathy) aren't really imperfections but our safeguards against cold logic and rationality, which can be catastrophic. An AI that is super advanced like HAL that works purely on rationality and logic and thinks itself to be the epitome of intelligence could very well conclude that humanity is a threat to itself and its advancement and decide to wipe us out in order to preserve the most intelligent and fastest advancing thing in the world.

I think that it's incredible that a movie that was released in 1968 can touch on topics that are incredibly relevant and concerning 58 years later.

What are your thoughts?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. A lot of early science fiction really explored the implications of AI - and lots of technology - in a much more thoughtful way than the people actually trying to implement the technology today. Like its all there in Asimov and others. This gets echoed with cyberpunk later which gets more critical about capitalism. 

We could all benefit from paying more attention not just to science fiction but all works in the past which shouldn't be dismissed out of hand and can still have a lot of deep relevance to our lives today.
2. "The fact that HAL tried to "sacrifice" every human on the spaceship because it thought that it was a completely faultless device and that its disconnection would lead to the end of a very important mission I think represents the danger of creating an emotionless entity without empathy (''the danger'' being the demise of humanity). I think Kubrick shows that our perceived imperfections (emotions and empathy) aren't really imperfections but our safeguards against cold logic and rationality, which can be catastrophic. An AI that is super advanced like HAL that works purely on rationality and logic and thinks itself to be the epitome of intelligence could very well conclude that humanity is a threat to itself and its advancement and decide to wipe us out in order to preserve the most intelligent and fastest advancing thing in the world."

  
I would just add that the movie begins with one group of hominids killing another. The way I see it, the whole thing is a kill or be killed story about how technological advancement gives some the upper hand, enabling domination and eventually extermination. HAL vs. Dave is another chapter of this story.
  - That is my interpretation as well. It’s a series of stories about the double-edged sword of technology and its impact on humanity. 
3. I think u/Vegetable_Hand8674 is right in their connection between HAL and weaponry. Kubrick's point is that technological advancement is driven by human desire to dominate others. So there's a direct link between the first human picking up the bone and realising he could use it as a weapon, and HAL. (When the apeman throws the bone in the air and we get the famous jump cut to a space craft, that craft is a nuclear missile - although I only know this from reading about the film, it's not immediately apparent to the viewer). So HAL has been invented to enable domination - domination is in its 'DNA', so to speak - and ultimately it's this that compels HAL to eliminate its human colleagues. The story is beyond prescient, as what we are currently seeing is an 'AI race', with nations desperately trying to advance AI faster than their rivals. They know that whoever is in the lead has an enormous military advantage. It's frankly terrifying. 

And, just to add, this theme goes even deeper. Note the first chapter of 2001 is titles 'The Dawn Of Man'. Kubrick's idea is that the drive for domination is not simply an aspect of humanity, but the defining feature of humanity. The moment the ape picks up the first weapon is the very moment humanity is born.
4. Yes, and it's far from the first to do it. People have thought about consciousness, the fate of humanity, transcendence, space, artificial intelligence etc for a long time.

RUR is from 1920, I Robot 1950, The Machine Stops 1909, Metropolis 1927. Then there's Mark Twain, Mary Shelley and Jules Verne, 19th century.
5. OP, since you seem to gravitate towards literature have you read the 2001: A Space Odyssey book by Arthur C. Clarke (whose short stories inspired the film)? The book was written with Kubrick alongside the making of the film. You might like having the story in a different format.
